hints: Focus on how the conditions for $\text{KMnO}_4$ change what happens to the C=C bond, mild versus vigorous oxidation.
Identify X first, cold dilute $\text{KMnO}_4$ adds two -OH groups across the double bond of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$ to give butane-2,3-diol.
Now think about which functional groups release $\text{H}_2$ with Na metal, and compare a diol with a carboxylic acid.
walkthrough:
**Find product X from mild oxidation**

Cold, dilute $\text{KMnO}_4$ does syn addition of two -OH groups across the double bond. It does not break the carbon chain.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3 + [O] + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH(OH)CH}_3$$
So X is butane-2,3-diol, a diol.

**Find product Y from vigorous oxidation**

Hot, concentrated, excess $\text{KMnO}_4$ cleaves the C=C bond completely. Each $\text{=CHCH}_3$ fragment is oxidised up to a carboxylic acid.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$
So Y is ethanoic acid, a carboxylic acid.

**Compare their test reactions**

X has alcohol -OH groups. Y has a carboxylic acid -COOH group. Both types contain an acidic H that reacts with very reactive sodium metal to give hydrogen gas.

$$2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_2$$
$$2\text{RCOOH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RCOONa} + \text{H}_2$$
So both X and Y react with sodium metal.

options.A: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine tests for a carbonyl group, aldehyde or ketone. X is a diol and Y is a carboxylic acid, so neither gives a positive orange precipitate. The statement that only one reacts is false.
options.B: Sodium hydroxide neutralises acids but not simple alcohols. Y (ethanoic acid) reacts to give sodium ethanoate and water, but X (butane-2,3-diol) is not acidic enough to react. So both reacting is false.
options.C: Both alcohols and carboxylic acids react with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen gas. X gives the alkoxide plus H2, and Y gives the carboxylate plus H2. So this statement is correct.
options.D: $\text{LiAlH}_4$ reduces a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Y ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) would give ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), not the 4-carbon diol X ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH(OH)CH}_3$). Reduction cannot rejoin the cleaved C-C bond.
